description_full: Matson, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the provision of ocean transportation and logistics services. It operates through two segments, Ocean Transportation and Logistics. The company offers ocean freight transportation services to the domestic non-contiguous economies of Hawaii, Alaska and Guam, and to other island economies in Micronesia; and transports dry containers of mixed commodities, refrigerated commodities, food products, beverages, building materials, automobiles, household goods, livestock, seafood, general sustenance cargo, e-commerce related goods, garments, consumer electronics, footwear, retail merchandise, and other merchandise. It also operates an expedited service from China to Long Beach, California, and various islands in the South Pacific, as well as Okinawa, Japan; and provides stevedoring, refrigerated cargo, inland transportation, container equipment maintenance, and other terminal services on the Hawaiian islands of Oahu, Hawaii, Maui, and Kauai, as well as in the Alaska terminal locations of Anchorage, Kodiak, and Dutch Harbor. In addition, the company provides multimodal transportation brokerage of domestic and international rail intermodal, long-haul and regional highway trucking, specialized hauling, flat-bed and project, less-than-truckload (LCL), and expedited freight services; LCL consolidation and freight forwarding services; warehousing, trans-loading, value-added packaging and distribution services; purchase order management, booking services, and non-vessel operating common carrier freight forwarding services. It serves the U.S. military, freight forwarders and non-vessel owning common carriers, retailers and consumer goods manufacturers, and other customers. The company was formerly known as Alexander & Baldwin Holdings, Inc. and changed its name to Matson, Inc. in June 2012. Matson, Inc. was founded in 1882 and is headquartered in Honolulu, Hawaii.

financial_summary: Matson, Inc. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $6.3B market cap on $3.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 9% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $154M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.23× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 74× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 5.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Priced near or above estimated fair value, so the margin of safety has been bid away
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Above-average short interest at 8.5% of float
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $11.6M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 8% over 3 months
Industrials ETF trading well below its long-term trend
Cyclical sectors like Industrials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sector_tailwinds: Valued at a 22% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
37 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 6pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.36x).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 110% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 12% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 0.95, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.43 vs 5y 0.93), so read it loosely.
About $59.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 37% in the 2020 crash, 51% in the 2022 bear market and 68% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $188 (margin of safety -13%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 23%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $120 to $296 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Industrials peers: cheaper on P/E 12.1 vs 23.3 and EV/EBITDA 10.3 vs 13.3, richer on P/FCF 41.2 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 123% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The 4 covering analysts target $277 on average, 31% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 16% earns above the cost of capital of 9.2%, but the 7pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.89).
It converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.23x.
ROE of 16% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.4x net debt to EBITDA ($141.9M of cash against $391.5M of debt), with interest covered 73.5x.
The current ratio of 0.89 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -8.3% over 3 years, 7.0% over 5 years and 5.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 18%).
At current returns, reinvesting 34% of profits supports about 5.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -13.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 2.7x depreciation (11.8% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 11, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 1.8%, and institutions hold 91%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (25 sales, net $11.6M sold).
It returns 5.5% a year to shareholders (4.8% in buybacks and 0.7% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 6.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 37 consecutive years, raising it 2.8% a year over the last five.
people: With about 4,170 employees, each generates about $802K of revenue, 2.2x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 4.8% a year.
That works out to $37K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.3M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
